items.title: Vaccines, immune memory and herd immunity
items.explainer: A vaccine trains the adaptive immune system to recognize a pathogen without the person having to survive the disease first. It presents an antigen, a recognizable piece or version of the pathogen, such as an inactivated virus, a purified protein, or genetic instructions for making a protein. B cells respond by producing antibodies that bind the antigen, and T cells learn to recognize infected cells. Crucially, some of these cells persist for years as memory cells. If the real pathogen arrives later, the memory cells respond within days instead of the week or more a first response takes, often clearing the infection before it causes serious illness. Vaccination also protects people who are not vaccinated. When enough of a population is immune, an infected person passes the disease on to fewer than one other person on average, and outbreaks fizzle out. The threshold depends on the basic reproduction number, R0, the average number of people one case infects in a fully susceptible population. Under simple assumptions the threshold is one minus one over R0. Measles, with an R0 commonly estimated between 12 and 18, needs immunity above 90 percent, which is why small declines in measles vaccination can quickly lead to outbreaks.

question.prompt: Under the simple model, what fraction of a population must be immune to stop sustained spread of a disease with R0 = 4?

options.text: 75 percent
25 percent
40 percent
100 percent

question.explanation: The threshold is 1 - 1/R0 = 1 - 1/4 = 0.75, so 75 percent of the population must be immune.

items.title: mRNA vaccines
items.explainer: An mRNA vaccine delivers genetic instructions rather than the antigen itself. A strand of messenger RNA encoding a viral protein, such as the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2, is packaged inside lipid nanoparticles, tiny fatty droplets that protect the fragile RNA and help it enter cells near the injection site. The cells' own ribosomes translate the mRNA into the protein, which the immune system then learns to recognize. The mRNA never enters the cell nucleus and cannot alter the cell's DNA, and it is broken down within days. Two technical problems held the approach back for decades. Injected RNA provoked strong inflammation and was quickly destroyed. Katalin Kariko and Drew Weissman showed in 2005 that replacing the nucleoside uridine with a modified version such as pseudouridine greatly reduced this inflammatory reaction while increasing protein production, work recognized with the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Improved lipid nanoparticle formulations solved the delivery problem. When COVID-19 emerged, the platform allowed vaccine candidates to be designed within days of the viral sequence being published. Because changing the target only requires changing the RNA sequence, mRNA is now being studied for influenza, other infectious diseases and personalized cancer vaccines.

question.prompt: What discovery by Kariko and Weissman helped make mRNA vaccines practical?

options.text: mRNA can integrate into the human genome for lasting protection
Modified nucleosides such as pseudouridine reduce inflammation and boost protein production
mRNA is stable at room temperature for years
Vaccines work without any immune response

question.explanation: Swapping uridine for modified nucleosides let the mRNA avoid triggering strong innate immune alarms, allowing it to be translated efficiently.

items.title: Antimicrobial resistance
items.explainer: Antimicrobial resistance occurs when bacteria and other microbes evolve the ability to survive drugs designed to kill them. It is natural selection in fast motion: when an antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria, any resistant ones survive and multiply, and resistance genes can then spread to other bacteria through horizontal gene transfer. Bacteria resist in a handful of ways. They can produce enzymes that destroy the drug, such as the beta-lactamases that break down penicillins; alter the drug's molecular target so it no longer binds; pump the drug out of the cell with efflux pumps; or reduce how much drug gets in. Misuse accelerates the problem: taking antibiotics for viral infections they cannot treat, stopping courses inconsistently against medical advice, and using large quantities in livestock all give resistant strains an advantage. The scale is substantial. A major study published in The Lancet in 2022 estimated that bacterial resistance was directly responsible for about 1.27 million deaths worldwide in 2019 and associated with millions more. Responses include antibiotic stewardship programs that reserve powerful drugs for when they are truly needed, better infection control in hospitals, faster diagnostics to identify the right drug, and incentives to develop new antibiotics, a market that has struggled commercially.

question.prompt: Why does taking antibiotics for a viral cold contribute to antibiotic resistance?

options.text: It makes the cold virus resistant to antibiotics
It weakens the patient's own antibodies permanently
It exposes the body's bacteria to the drug, favoring resistant strains, while doing nothing against the virus
It has no effect on resistance at all

question.explanation: Antibiotics do not act on viruses, but they still kill susceptible bacteria in the body, giving any resistant bacteria a survival advantage.

items.title: Monoclonal antibodies
items.explainer: Antibodies are Y-shaped proteins that bind specific molecular targets with high precision. A natural immune response produces a mixture of antibodies from many different B cells, each recognizing a slightly different part of an antigen. A monoclonal antibody is a single antibody type produced by clones of one cell, so every molecule binds exactly the same target. In 1975 Georges Kohler and Cesar Milstein developed the hybridoma technique, fusing an antibody-producing B cell with an immortal myeloma cell to create a cell line that makes one antibody indefinitely; they shared a Nobel Prize in 1984. Early mouse antibodies triggered immune reactions in patients, so later methods produced chimeric, humanized and finally fully human antibodies. The naming convention reflects this history: drug names ending in '-ximab' are chimeric and those ending in '-zumab' are humanized. Monoclonal antibodies are now among the best-selling medicines. They block inflammatory signals in rheumatoid arthritis, mark cancer cells for destruction, release brakes on the immune system in cancer immunotherapy, and deliver toxic payloads directly to tumors as antibody-drug conjugates. They are also everyday laboratory tools and the basis of rapid diagnostic tests. Because they are large proteins, most must be injected or infused rather than swallowed.

question.prompt: What distinguishes a monoclonal antibody preparation from the antibodies produced in a natural immune response?

options.text: It contains antibodies against many different pathogens
It is made of DNA rather than protein
It can be taken as a pill because it survives digestion
All its molecules come from one cell clone and bind exactly the same target

question.explanation: A natural response is polyclonal, a mixture of antibodies from many B cells. A monoclonal preparation is identical antibodies from a single clone.

items.title: Oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes
items.explainer: Cancer is fundamentally a disease of genes that control cell growth and division. Two broad classes matter most. Oncogenes are mutated versions of normal genes, called proto-oncogenes, that promote cell growth. A mutation can lock such a gene in the 'on' position, like a car accelerator stuck to the floor; the RAS gene family is a common example. Because one altered copy is enough to push growth, these mutations act dominantly. Tumor suppressor genes are the brakes. They halt the cell cycle, repair DNA, or trigger cell death when damage is severe. The p53 gene, sometimes called the guardian of the genome, is mutated in roughly half of human cancers. Losing a tumor suppressor usually requires both copies to be disabled. Alfred Knudson's 1971 'two-hit hypothesis', based on the childhood eye cancer retinoblastoma, explained why: children who inherit one defective copy of the RB1 gene need only one further mutation, so they develop tumors earlier and more often, frequently in both eyes. Inherited mutations in tumor suppressors such as BRCA1 and BRCA2 similarly raise lifetime cancer risk. Most cancers accumulate several such mutations over years, which is one reason cancer risk rises with age.

question.prompt: According to Knudson's two-hit hypothesis, why do children who inherit one defective RB1 gene develop retinoblastoma more often?

options.text: They already carry one hit, so a single further mutation can disable the gene completely
The inherited gene acts as a dominant oncogene
Their immune system cannot recognize eye cells
The disease is caused by a virus passed from the parent

question.explanation: Tumor suppressors usually need both copies inactivated. Inheriting one defective copy means only one more mutation is needed in a retinal cell.

items.title: Immune checkpoint inhibitors
items.explainer: The immune system has built-in brakes, called checkpoints, that stop T cells from attacking the body's own tissues and keep immune responses from running out of control. Two important checkpoint proteins on T cells are CTLA-4 and PD-1. When PD-1 binds its partner molecule, PD-L1, on another cell, the T cell is told to stand down. Many tumors exploit this by displaying PD-L1 on their surface, effectively telling attacking T cells to switch off. Checkpoint inhibitors are monoclonal antibodies that block these brakes, releasing the immune system to attack the cancer. James Allison, working on CTLA-4, and Tasuku Honjo, working on PD-1, shared the 2018 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this approach. The results transformed treatment of some cancers. A subset of patients with advanced melanoma, which was once almost uniformly fatal within months, now survive for many years, and checkpoint inhibitors are used in lung, kidney, bladder and other cancers. The approach has clear limits. Only a minority of patients respond in many cancer types, and researchers are still learning to predict who will. Because the brakes are released body-wide, side effects can include autoimmune inflammation of the skin, gut, liver, lungs or hormone glands.

question.prompt: How do PD-1 checkpoint inhibitors help the immune system fight cancer?

options.text: They directly poison dividing cancer cells
They block an inhibitory signal that tumors use to switch off T cells
They suppress the immune system to reduce inflammation
They repair mutated DNA in tumor cells

question.explanation: Tumors can display PD-L1 to engage PD-1 and silence T cells. Blocking that interaction releases the brake so T cells can attack.

items.title: CAR-T cell therapy
items.explainer: CAR-T cell therapy turns a patient's own immune cells into a living drug. T cells are collected from the patient's blood and genetically engineered, usually with a modified virus, to express a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. The receptor combines the targeting part of an antibody, which recognizes a specific protein on cancer cells, with signaling components that activate the T cell when it binds. The engineered cells are multiplied in the laboratory and infused back into the patient, typically after chemotherapy that makes room for them in the immune system. Once inside, they seek out and kill cells carrying the target and can keep multiplying, sometimes persisting for years. The first CAR-T therapy approved in the United States, in 2017, targeted the CD19 protein found on B cells and treated children and young adults with a form of acute lymphoblastic leukemia that had resisted other treatments. Several products for leukemias, lymphomas and multiple myeloma have followed. Serious risks include cytokine release syndrome, a dangerous surge of immune signaling, and neurological toxicity. Each dose is custom-made for one patient, which makes the therapy very expensive, and solid tumors have proved much harder to treat than blood cancers.

question.prompt: What is the chimeric antigen receptor in CAR-T therapy designed to do?

options.text: Block T cells from dividing after infusion
Replace the patient's red blood cells
Let engineered T cells recognize a chosen protein on cancer cells and activate on binding
Deliver chemotherapy drugs directly into the bloodstream

question.explanation: The CAR fuses antibody-like targeting with T-cell activation signals, redirecting the patient's T cells against cells carrying the target antigen.

items.title: Sensitivity, specificity and predictive value
items.explainer: Diagnostic tests are judged by two properties of the test itself. Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive; specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative. A highly sensitive test rarely misses true cases, which makes it useful for ruling disease out, while a highly specific test rarely raises false alarms. What a patient actually wants to know is different: given a positive result, how likely is it that I have the disease? That is the positive predictive value, and it depends heavily on how common the disease is in the population being tested. Consider a test with 99 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity used to screen a population where 1 percent have the disease. Of 10,000 people, 100 are sick and 99 of them test positive. Of the 9,900 healthy people, 5 percent, or 495, also test positive. So only 99 of 594 positive results are true positives, a predictive value of about 17 percent. This base-rate effect is a direct application of Bayes' theorem. It explains why screening for rare conditions produces many false positives and why positive screening results are usually confirmed with a second, more specific test.

question.prompt: A test with 99 percent sensitivity and 95 percent specificity is used where 1 percent of people have the disease. Roughly what fraction of positive results are true positives?

options.text: About 99 percent
About 95 percent
About 50 percent
About 17 percent

question.explanation: Per 10,000 people: 99 true positives and 495 false positives, so 99 / 594 is about 17 percent. Low prevalence drags the predictive value down.

items.title: The human microbiome
items.explainer: The human body hosts trillions of microbes, mostly bacteria, living on the skin, in the mouth and above all in the large intestine. Together they are called the microbiota, and their combined genes the microbiome. A widely repeated claim held that bacterial cells outnumber human cells ten to one, but a careful 2016 estimate put the numbers at roughly 38 trillion bacteria and 30 trillion human cells, a ratio closer to one to one. Gut bacteria perform jobs our own cells cannot. They ferment dietary fiber into short-chain fatty acids that nourish the cells lining the colon, synthesize certain vitamins such as vitamin K, help train the immune system, and occupy space that harmful microbes might otherwise colonize. Disrupting this community can cause disease. Broad-spectrum antibiotics can wipe out protective species and allow Clostridioides difficile to take over, causing severe, recurrent diarrhea. Transplanting stool from a healthy donor restores a diverse community and cures most recurrent cases, one of the clearest demonstrations that the microbiome matters for health. Associations have also been reported with obesity, inflammatory bowel disease, allergies and even mood, but for many of these it remains unclear whether changes in the microbiome are a cause of disease or a consequence of it.

question.prompt: Which treatment most clearly demonstrated that restoring the gut microbiome can cure a disease?

options.text: Fecal microbiota transplant for recurrent C. difficile infection
Antibiotics for viral infections
Vitamin K injections for newborns
Probiotic yogurt for seasonal allergies

question.explanation: Transplanting a healthy donor's stool restores microbial diversity and resolves most cases of recurrent C. difficile infection.

items.title: Randomized controlled trials and blinding
items.explainer: The randomized controlled trial, or RCT, is the standard method for testing whether a medical treatment works. Participants are assigned at random to receive either the treatment or a comparison, which may be a placebo or the current standard treatment. Randomization is the crucial step. It balances the groups, on average, for every factor that might affect the outcome, including factors nobody has thought to measure, such as diet, genetics or motivation. Any difference in outcomes can then be attributed to the treatment rather than to pre-existing differences between the groups, something observational studies cannot guarantee. Blinding adds protection against bias in expectations and judgments. In a single-blind trial participants do not know which group they are in; in a double-blind trial neither the participants nor the researchers assessing them know. This matters because beliefs change behavior and perception: patients given a placebo often report real improvements, and doctors who know who got the drug may judge outcomes differently. Trials are also registered in advance with their planned outcomes, so results cannot quietly be reported only for whichever measures looked best. RCTs have limits too. They can be expensive, slow, unethical for some questions, and their volunteers may differ from the broader population of patients.

question.prompt: What is the main advantage of random assignment in a clinical trial?

options.text: It guarantees that the treatment will work
It balances the groups on average for both measured and unmeasured factors
It removes the need for a control group
It ensures every participant receives the active drug

question.explanation: Randomization makes the groups comparable in expectation, including on unknown confounders, so outcome differences can be attributed to the treatment.

items.title: Innate and adaptive immunity
items.explainer: The immune system has two arms that work together. The innate immune system is the fast, general first line of defense. It includes physical barriers such as skin and mucus, white blood cells such as neutrophils and macrophages that engulf invaders, and proteins that punch holes in bacteria. Innate cells recognize broad patterns common to many microbes, such as parts of bacterial cell walls or viral RNA, using pattern recognition receptors like the Toll-like receptors. They respond within minutes to hours, but the response is the same every time. The adaptive immune system is slower to start but highly specific, and it remembers. Its B cells and T cells each carry receptors that recognize one particular molecular shape, and the body makes millions of different versions by shuffling gene segments. When a cell meets its matching antigen, it multiplies into an army of identical clones. B cells make antibodies that tag invaders; helper T cells coordinate the response; and cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells. A first adaptive response takes a week or more to build, but memory cells left behind make a second encounter far faster and stronger. The two arms are linked: dendritic cells of the innate system present antigens that switch on T cells.

question.prompt: Which feature belongs to the adaptive immune system but not the innate one?

options.text: Physical barriers such as skin
Immediate response within minutes
Immunological memory of specific antigens
Recognition of broad microbial patterns

question.explanation: Adaptive B and T cells recognize specific antigens and leave memory cells that speed up later responses; innate defences respond the same way each time.

items.title: Inflammation
items.explainer: Inflammation is the body's immediate response to injury or infection. Its classic signs, described since ancient times, are redness, heat, swelling and pain, with loss of function often added as a fifth. They all follow from what happens in the tissue. Damaged cells and immune sentinels such as mast cells and macrophages release signaling molecules, including histamine, prostaglandins and cytokines. These widen nearby blood vessels, increasing blood flow, which causes redness and heat, and make the vessel walls leaky, so fluid and proteins seep into the tissue and cause swelling. Some of the same molecules sensitize nerve endings, producing pain that discourages use of the injured part. White blood cells, first neutrophils and later macrophages, squeeze out of the vessels and move towards the site to destroy microbes and clear debris, after which the inflammation should resolve and repair begins. Acute inflammation is protective. Problems arise when it fails to switch off. Chronic, low-grade inflammation is involved in atherosclerosis, type 2 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis and some cancers. Common anti-inflammatory drugs act on these signals: ibuprofen and aspirin block the cyclooxygenase enzymes that make prostaglandins, and corticosteroids broadly suppress the production of inflammatory cytokines.

question.prompt: How do drugs such as ibuprofen reduce inflammation?

options.text: By killing bacteria
By increasing histamine release
By stimulating antibody production
By blocking cyclooxygenase enzymes that make prostaglandins

question.explanation: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase, cutting production of the prostaglandins that drive pain, swelling and fever.

items.title: How antibiotics work
items.explainer: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them growing by attacking structures and processes that bacteria have but human cells lack or build differently, so the drug harms the microbe far more than the patient. Penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928, and related drugs called beta-lactams block the enzymes that build the bacterial cell wall, a mesh of peptidoglycan that human cells do not have; without it, growing bacteria burst. Other antibiotics target the bacterial ribosome, which differs in structure from ours: tetracyclines, macrolides such as azithromycin, and aminoglycosides all stop bacteria making proteins. Fluoroquinolones such as ciprofloxacin block the enzymes bacteria use to untangle their DNA during copying, and sulfonamides interfere with the bacterial production of folate, a vitamin that humans get from food. Antibiotics are described as bactericidal if they kill bacteria and bacteriostatic if they only stop them multiplying, leaving the immune system to finish the job. Some act on a narrow range of bacteria, others on a broad spectrum. Antibiotics have no effect on viruses, which have no cell walls or ribosomes of their own, so they do not help colds or flu. Unnecessary use encourages resistant bacteria and also disrupts the helpful bacteria of the gut.

question.prompt: Why are antibiotics ineffective against the common cold?

options.text: Colds are caused by viruses, which lack the bacterial structures antibiotics target
Cold viruses are all resistant to antibiotics
Antibiotics cannot reach the nose
Colds are caused by fungi

question.explanation: Antibiotics attack bacterial cell walls, ribosomes and enzymes; viruses use the host's machinery, so these drugs have nothing to hit.

items.title: Autoimmunity
items.explainer: An autoimmune disease occurs when the immune system attacks the body's own tissues. Normally this is prevented by tolerance. While T cells mature in the thymus, those that react strongly to the body's own proteins are eliminated, a process called central tolerance. Some self-reactive cells escape, so peripheral tolerance adds further safeguards, most importantly regulatory T cells that suppress immune responses, an idea for which Shimon Sakaguchi, Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell shared the 2025 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. When these controls fail, autoantibodies and self-reactive T cells damage tissue. In type 1 diabetes, T cells destroy the insulin-producing beta cells of the pancreas. In rheumatoid arthritis, the lining of the joints is inflamed. In multiple sclerosis, the fatty myelin insulation around nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord is attacked, and in lupus, antibodies against components of the cell nucleus cause damage in many organs. The causes combine genetic susceptibility, especially particular variants of the HLA genes that present antigens to T cells, with environmental triggers such as infections; for example, infection with the Epstein-Barr virus greatly raises the risk of multiple sclerosis. Autoimmune diseases are more common in women. Treatments range from broad immune suppression to targeted biologic drugs that block specific inflammatory signals.

question.prompt: What is the role of regulatory T cells in preventing autoimmune disease?

options.text: They make antibodies against microbes
They suppress self-reactive immune responses as part of peripheral tolerance
They destroy the thymus
They produce insulin

question.explanation: Regulatory T cells restrain immune cells that escaped central tolerance, keeping attacks on the body's own tissues in check.

items.title: Type 1 and type 2 diabetes
items.explainer: Diabetes is a condition in which blood glucose stays too high because the hormone insulin is missing or not working properly. Insulin, made by the beta cells of the pancreas, tells muscle, fat and liver cells to take up glucose from the blood after a meal. In type 1 diabetes, the immune system destroys the beta cells, so the body makes little or no insulin. It usually begins in childhood or young adulthood, and people with it need insulin injections or a pump to survive; before Frederick Banting and Charles Best isolated insulin in 1921, it was fatal. Type 2 diabetes, which accounts for about 90 percent of cases, starts with insulin resistance: cells respond less to insulin, so the pancreas has to make more, until it can no longer keep up. It is strongly linked to excess body fat, physical inactivity, age and family history, and it can often be managed for years with lifestyle changes and tablets such as metformin before insulin is needed. Newer drugs that mimic the gut hormone GLP-1 lower glucose and also cause weight loss. Over time, high blood glucose damages blood vessels and nerves, raising the risk of heart disease, kidney failure, blindness and amputations. Doctors track control with the HbA1c test.

question.prompt: What is the main underlying problem in type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of all beta cells
Too much insulin from the liver
Insulin resistance, with the pancreas eventually unable to compensate
A viral infection of the pancreas

question.explanation: Type 2 diabetes begins with cells responding poorly to insulin; type 1 is the autoimmune loss of beta cells.

items.title: Atherosclerosis
items.explainer: Atherosclerosis is the build-up of fatty plaques inside the walls of arteries, and it is the underlying cause of most heart attacks and many strokes. It begins with damage to the endothelium, the thin inner lining of the artery, from factors such as high blood pressure, smoking and high blood sugar. Low-density lipoprotein, or LDL, the particle that carries cholesterol in the blood, slips into the damaged wall and becomes chemically modified. Immune cells called macrophages move in to engulf it and swell into lipid-laden foam cells. Over years, this inflammatory process builds a plaque with a fatty core covered by a fibrous cap. Large plaques can narrow the artery enough to cause chest pain during exercise, known as angina. The greater danger, though, is rupture. If the fibrous cap tears, the plaque's contents come into contact with blood, a clot forms on the spot, and it can block the artery completely within minutes, starving heart or brain tissue of oxygen. This is why heart attacks often strike people whose arteries were not severely narrowed. Prevention focuses on lowering LDL cholesterol, most often with statins, which block the liver enzyme HMG-CoA reductase, and on controlling blood pressure, stopping smoking and managing diabetes.

question.prompt: What usually triggers the sudden blockage that causes a heart attack?

options.text: A plaque slowly closes the artery over decades
The heart muscle stops producing cholesterol
The artery wall becomes too elastic
A plaque ruptures and a blood clot forms on it

question.explanation: Rupture of a plaque's fibrous cap exposes its contents to blood, forming a clot that can block the artery within minutes.

items.title: Gene therapy and viral vectors
items.explainer: Gene therapy treats disease by delivering genetic material into a patient's cells, usually to supply a working copy of a faulty gene or to switch a harmful one off. The hard part is delivery. DNA cannot easily cross cell membranes or reach the nucleus by itself, so most therapies use viruses that have been stripped of their disease-causing genes and loaded with the therapeutic gene instead. Adeno-associated viruses, or AAVs, are the most common vectors for treatments given directly into the body. They cause no known disease, infect many tissue types and mostly remain in the nucleus without inserting into chromosomes, so the effect can last for years in cells that do not divide. Onasemnogene abeparvovec, approved in 2019, uses an AAV to deliver the SMN1 gene to babies with spinal muscular atrophy. Lentiviruses, derived from HIV, do insert their cargo into chromosomes, so they are used to modify cells outside the body that will then divide, such as blood stem cells and the T cells used in CAR-T therapy. Gene therapy has had setbacks. In 1999 Jesse Gelsinger died from an immune reaction to a vector, and early trials with other inserting viruses caused leukemia. Immune responses to the vector and very high prices remain major challenges.

question.prompt: Why are lentiviral vectors used for cells that will go on dividing, such as blood stem cells?

options.text: They insert their cargo into the chromosomes, so the gene is copied into every daughter cell
They cannot infect human cells
They are destroyed after one day
They only work in the brain

question.explanation: Integration into chromosomes means the therapeutic gene is passed on at each division; non-integrating AAV genomes are diluted out in dividing cells.

items.title: Induced pluripotent stem cells
items.explainer: Pluripotent stem cells can become any cell type in the body, from neurons to heart muscle. Until 2006 the main source was human embryos, which raised ethical objections and created immune-matching problems for transplants. That year Shinya Yamanaka and Kazutoshi Takahashi showed that ordinary adult skin cells from mice could be reprogrammed into a pluripotent state by switching on just four genes, Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc, now called the Yamanaka factors. They did the same with human cells in 2007. These induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPSCs, behave much like embryonic stem cells. Yamanaka shared the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with John Gurdon, who had shown decades earlier that a frog egg could reprogram the nucleus of a mature cell. iPSCs have several uses. Researchers can take cells from a patient with a genetic disease, turn them into the affected cell type, and study the disease or test drugs in a dish. Because the cells come from the patient, transplants made from them could in principle avoid immune rejection. The first clinical trials have tested iPSC-derived retinal cells for macular degeneration and dopamine-producing neurons for Parkinson's disease. A key safety concern is that leftover undifferentiated cells could form tumors.

question.prompt: What did Yamanaka's 2006 discovery show?

options.text: That embryos are needed to make any stem cell
That adult cells can be reprogrammed into pluripotent stem cells by switching on four genes
That stem cells cannot become neurons
That frog eggs can be grown from skin cells

question.explanation: Switching on Oct4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc reprogrammed mature cells into a pluripotent state, without embryos.

items.title: Polymerase chain reaction
items.explainer: The polymerase chain reaction, or PCR, makes millions to billions of copies of a chosen stretch of DNA in a few hours, so that even a trace amount can be detected and studied. Kary Mullis devised it in 1983 and shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for it. The reaction mixture contains the sample DNA, a heat-stable DNA polymerase, the four DNA building blocks, and two short primers, single-stranded pieces of DNA that match the two ends of the target region. A machine called a thermal cycler then repeats three steps. Heating to about 95 °C separates the two strands of the DNA. Cooling to around 50 to 65 °C lets the primers bind to their matching sequences. Warming to about 72 °C lets the polymerase extend the primers, copying the target. Each cycle roughly doubles the number of copies, so 30 cycles can in principle produce about a billion. The method became practical with Taq polymerase, from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus, which survives the repeated heating. Quantitative PCR measures how quickly the copies build up to estimate how much target was there at the start, and reverse transcription PCR first copies RNA into DNA, which is how COVID-19 tests detected the RNA genome of the virus.

question.prompt: Why was Taq polymerase important for making PCR practical?

options.text: It makes primers automatically
It copies RNA directly into protein
It survives the repeated heating to about 95 °C needed to separate DNA strands
It works only at room temperature

question.explanation: Taq polymerase, from a hot-spring bacterium, withstands each high-temperature step, so it need not be replaced every cycle.

items.title: Absolute and relative risk
items.explainer: Medical news often reports that a treatment cuts the risk of something by half, but that figure means little without knowing how common the problem was to begin with. Relative risk compares the risk in a treated group with the risk in an untreated group. If 2 in 1,000 untreated people have a heart attack over five years and 1 in 1,000 treated people do, the relative risk is 0.5, a 50 percent relative risk reduction. The absolute risk reduction is the plain difference in risk: 2 minus 1 per 1,000, or 0.1 percentage points. Both numbers are true, but they leave very different impressions. A related measure is the number needed to treat, the number of people who must receive the treatment for one of them to benefit, which is one divided by the absolute risk reduction; here it is 1,000. If the same drug were given to a high-risk group in which 200 in 1,000 would have a heart attack, the same 50 percent relative reduction would prevent 100 heart attacks per 1,000 people, and the number needed to treat would be 10. That is why guidelines target treatments at people with a higher baseline risk. Good reporting gives absolute risks alongside relative ones, together with the harms of the treatment.

question.prompt: A drug reduces risk of a stroke from 4% to 3%. What is the number needed to treat?
question.explanation: The absolute risk reduction is 1 percentage point (0.01), so NNT = 1/0.01 = 100.
